clinicalPearls: Two gallstone types: cholesterol stones (>90% in Western countries, contain >50% cholesterol monohydrate) and pigment stones (mainly calcium bilirubinate, <20% cholesterol, split into 'black' and 'brown' types) (p.2728-2729).

Cholesterol gallstones arise from three defects: (1) bile supersaturation with cholesterol, (2) accelerated nucleation of cholesterol monohydrate crystals, and (3) gallbladder hypomotility/stasis (p.2729).

Black pigment stones associate with chronic hemolysis, alcohol-related cirrhosis, Gilbert's syndrome, cystic fibrosis, and ileal disease/resection/bypass; brown pigment stones form secondary to chronic biliary infection/parasitism with deconjugation of bilirubin (p.2729).

Biliary colic is the most specific symptom: a steady (not intermittent) severe ache or fullness in the epigastrium/RUQ radiating to the interscapular area, right scapula, or shoulder, lasting 30 min to 5 h; the word 'colic' is a misnomer (p.2730-2731).

60-80% of asymptomatic gallstones remain asymptomatic over up to 25 years; symptom development is ~2-4% per year (falling to 1-2% later) and yearly complication rate is ~0.1-0.3%, so prophylactic cholecystectomy is not warranted (p.2731).
Ultrasound is the procedure of choice for detecting gallstones (>95% accuracy) and can identify stones as small as 1.5 mm using acoustic shadowing criteria (p.2730).

Biliary sludge (lecithin-cholesterol liquid crystals, cholesterol monohydrate crystals, calcium bilirubinate, mucin) shifts with posture but does NOT cast an acoustic shadow, distinguishing it from stones; it can be a gallstone precursor (p.2730).

Acute cholecystitis usually follows cystic duct obstruction by a stone; Murphy's sign (inspiratory arrest on RUQ palpation) is characteristic, and the triad of sudden RUQ tenderness, fever, and leukocytosis is highly suggestive (p.2732-2733).

Charcot's triad (biliary pain, jaundice, spiking fevers with chills) characterizes acute cholangitis; suppurative cholangitis with a completely obstructed duct under pressure causes mental confusion, bacteremia, and septic shock (Reynolds' pentad features) (p.2735).

Choledocholithiasis (CBD stones) occurs in ~10-15% of patients with cholelithiasis; incidence rises with age (up to 25% of elderly at cholecystectomy); most are cholesterol stones that migrated from the gallbladder (p.2735).

MRCP is the first choice to assess for choledocholithiasis (comparable sensitivity/specificity to ERCP); ERCP is the cholangiogram of choice when intervention is needed and ERCP with sphincterotomy is preferred for both diagnosis and therapy of bacterial cholangitis (p.2736, 2735).

PBC: female-predominant (~50 yr median age) autoimmune disease with portal inflammation and necrosis of cholangiocytes in small/medium bile ducts; antimitochondrial antibodies (AMA) present in ~95%; key symptoms are fatigue and pruritus (Harrison 22e ch.355 p.2711).

PSC is strongly associated with inflammatory bowel disease (60-80%, predominantly ulcerative colitis); cholangiography shows multifocal strictures with intervening normal/dilated segments producing a 'beaded' appearance; pANCA positive in ~65% (ch.357 p.2737; ch.355 p.2712).

Cholangiocarcinoma is classified as intrahepatic (~20-30%), perihilar (~50-60%), and distal (~20-30%); PSC is a clear risk factor for iCCA and pCCA with a 5-10% lifetime incidence, and is a relative contraindication to liver transplantation (ch.87 p.667; ch.355 p.2712).

Gallbladder cancer: cholelithiasis is the major risk factor but <1% of patients with gallstones develop it; polyps >=10 mm are at risk of transformation; early cases are found incidentally at cholecystectomy and symptoms (jaundice, pain, weight loss) indicate advanced disease (ch.87 p.670).
harrison.pathophysiology: Bile flow depends on sphincter of Oddi tone and cholecystokinin (CCK)-mediated gallbladder contraction after fatty/amino-acid meals. Gallstones form from abnormal bile composition. Cholesterol stones (>90% in Western countries) require three converging defects: hepatic hypersecretion of cholesterol producing lithogenic/supersaturated bile (driven by obesity, metabolic syndrome, estrogens, rapid weight loss, age, CYP7A1 or MDR3/ABCB4 gene defects, ABCG5/G8 variants), accelerated nucleation of cholesterol monohydrate crystals (excess pronucleating mucin/immunoglobulins vs deficient antinucleating apolipoproteins), and gallbladder hypomotility with stasis (fasting, TPN, pregnancy, octreotide). Pigment stones contain calcium bilirubinate: black stones from chronic hemolysis, cirrhosis, Gilbert's, cystic fibrosis, or ileal disease (enterohepatic bilirubin recycling); brown stones from deconjugation of bilirubin by bacterial beta-glucuronidase in chronically infected/parasitized bile. Symptoms arise when stones obstruct the cystic duct (cholecystitis) or migrate into the CBD (choledocholithiasis) causing biliary obstruction, cholangitis, or gallstone pancreatitis as they pass through the ampulla of Vater. PBC and PSC are chronic cholestatic syndromes from immune-mediated destruction of bile ducts (small/medium ducts in PBC; entire biliary tree in PSC) progressing to biliary cirrhosis and portal hypertension.
additionalDifferentials: Acalculous cholecystitis (5-14% of acute cholecystitis; associated with prolonged fasting, severe trauma/burns, postpartum, major nonbiliary surgery, TPN) (p.2733)
Acalculous cholecystopathy / biliary dyskinesia (gallbladder ejection fraction <40% on CCK cholescintigraphy reproducing pain) (p.2733)
Sphincter of Oddi dysfunction (stenosis or dyskinesia) (p.2734)
Choledochal cysts and Caroli's disease / congenital biliary ectasia (recurrent cholangitis, increased cholangiocarcinoma risk) (p.2735)
Benign bile duct strictures (post-surgical, ~1 in 500 cholecystectomies) (p.2737)
Extrinsic bile duct compression (most commonly carcinoma of the head of the pancreas) (p.2737)
IgG4-associated cholangitis (mimics PSC; elevated serum IgG4; steroid-responsive) (p.2737)
Postcholecystectomy syndrome (overlooked reflux esophagitis, peptic ulcer, IBS, retained stones, bile-salt diarrhea) (p.2734)
infectionMimics: Acute (ascending) cholangitis from bacterial superinfection of obstructed bile (p.2735)
Hepatobiliary parasitism (Clonorchis sinensis, Opisthorchis viverrini/felineus, Fasciola hepatica, Ascaris, Echinococcus) causing recurrent pyogenic cholangitis (p.2737)
Emphysematous cholecystitis from gas-producing organisms (Clostridium welchii/perfringens, E. coli) in elderly/diabetic patients (p.2733)
AIDS cholangiopathy (Cryptosporidium, Mycobacterium avium-intracellulare, CMV, Microsporidia, Isospora) mimicking sclerosing cholangitis (p.2737)
nonInfectiousMimics: Malignant biliary obstruction (pancreatic head carcinoma, cholangiocarcinoma, ampullary tumor) - Courvoisier's law: a palpably enlarged gallbladder suggests malignancy rather than stones (p.2736)
Functional/vague dyspepsia, eructation, flatulence after fatty meals - common with or without gallstones but not specific for biliary calculi (p.2731)
Other postcholecystectomy nonbiliary disorders (reflux esophagitis, peptic ulcer, pancreatitis, irritable bowel syndrome) (p.2734)
additionalInvestigations: Ultrasound - procedure of choice for gallstone detection (>95%), gallbladder wall thickening, pericholecystic fluid, dilated ducts (p.2730, 2733)
MRCP - first choice for choledocholithiasis and the cholangiographic technique of choice in suspected PSC (beaded ducts) (p.2736-2737)
ERCP with endoscopic sphincterotomy - diagnostic and therapeutic for CBD stones and bacterial cholangitis (p.2735-2736)
Cholescintigraphy (HIDA/DISIDA) - confirms cystic duct obstruction / acute cholecystitis; CCK-stimulated for ejection fraction in acalculous cholecystopathy (p.2730, 2733)
Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) - most sensitive for ampullary stones and head-of-pancreas pathology; detects microlithiasis (p.2736)
Plain abdominal film - calcified stones, porcelain gallbladder, limey bile, emphysematous cholecystitis, gallstone ileus (pneumobilia) (p.2730)
Serum bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase - elevation suggests common duct stone; ALP rise often precedes jaundice (p.2731, 2736)

AMA (and sp100/gp210 if AMA-negative) for PBC; IgM elevation; serum IgG4 to exclude IgG4 cholangitis; pANCA in PSC; CA 19-9 for cholangiocarcinoma surveillance in PSC (ch.355 p.2711, ch.357 p.2737, ch.87 p.667)
Endoscopic brushing of biliary strictures (more accurate than bile cytology alone) in suspected neoplastic stricture, especially in PSC (p.2737)
redFlags: Biliary pain persisting beyond 5 h - raises suspicion of acute cholecystitis (p.2731)
Fever or chills (rigors) with biliary pain - implies a complication (cholecystitis, pancreatitis, or cholangitis) (p.2731)
Charcot's triad (biliary pain, jaundice, spiking fevers/chills) - acute cholangitis (p.2735)
Mental confusion, bacteremia, septic shock (suppurative cholangitis) - mortality approaches 100% without prompt drainage (p.2735)
Serum bilirubin >=342 micromol/L (20 mg/dL) - suggests neoplastic rather than calculous obstruction (p.2736)
Painless jaundice and/or a palpably enlarged gallbladder (Courvoisier) - points to malignancy (p.2736)
Sudden transient relief of RUQ pain followed by generalized peritonitis - free gallbladder perforation (~30% mortality) (p.2733)
Pruritus preceding jaundice in PBC - indicates severe disease and poor prognosis (ch.355 p.2711)
New/rising bilirubin or dominant stricture in PSC - concern for cholangiocarcinoma (ch.355 p.2712; ch.87 p.667)
harrison.prognosis: Most asymptomatic gallstones stay silent (60-80% over up to 25 years); cumulative death risk on expectant management is small. Laparoscopic cholecystectomy is the gold standard with complications ~4%, conversion ~5%, death rate <0.1%, and bile duct injury 0.2-0.6%; it relieves preoperative symptoms in 75-90%. Acute cholecystitis: ~75% remit medically within 2-7 days but ~25% recur within 1 year and 60% within 6 years; free perforation carries ~30% mortality and suppurative cholangitis approaches 100% mortality without drainage. PSC is progressive with a median survival of 12-18 years regardless of therapy and is a common indication for liver transplantation; small-duct PSC has a significantly better prognosis. PBC: UDCA slows but does not reverse disease; transplantation for decompensated cirrhosis. Cholangiocarcinoma has a 5-year survival of ~10%; gallbladder cancer is curable (5-yr survival 60-90%) only when local and resected (~20% of patients), with median survival 10-12 months in advanced disease (ch.357 p.2731-2737; ch.355 p.2711-2712; ch.87 p.667-670).
pitfalls: 'Biliary colic' is a misnomer - the pain is steady, not intermittent (p.2731)
Vague postprandial dyspepsia, eructation, and flatulence are not specific for gallstones and should not be confused with biliary pain (p.2731)

Pigment stones do NOT respond to UDCA dissolution therapy, and stones >10 mm rarely dissolve - only ~10% of symptomatic patients are dissolution candidates with 30-50% recurrence over 3-5 years (p.2731-2732)
Jaundice is unusual early in acute cholecystitis; its presence (or bilirubin >5 mg/dL) should prompt suspicion of a CBD stone (p.2732, 2736)
Missing Mirizzi's syndrome preoperatively risks CBD injury at surgery (p.2733)
AMA is negative in 5-10% of PBC - liver biopsy and sp100/gp210 are needed, and PSC should be excluded by cholangiography (ch.355 p.2711)
Every patient diagnosed with sclerosing cholangitis should have serum IgG4 checked to exclude IgG4-associated (secondary) cholangitis, especially without IBD (p.2737)
Routine prophylactic cholecystectomy in asymptomatic stones (including young patients and diabetics) is not warranted (p.2731)
The carcinoma risk of porcelain gallbladder has been challenged; cholecystectomy is no longer absolute and surveillance is acceptable (p.2734)
harrison.severityClassification: Stone-based spectrum: asymptomatic gallstones -> biliary colic (cystic duct/CBD obstruction) -> acute cholecystitis -> complications (empyema, hydrops/mucocele, gangrene, perforation, fistula with gallstone ileus, emphysematous cholecystitis, Mirizzi's syndrome). CBD stone (choledocholithiasis) complications: cholangitis (nonsuppurative vs suppurative), obstructive jaundice, gallstone pancreatitis, secondary biliary cirrhosis. Cholangitis severity by Charcot's triad (pain + jaundice + fever/chills) advancing to suppurative cholangitis (adds confusion + septic shock). PBC has four histologic stages from chronic nonsuppurative destructive cholangitis to cirrhosis. PSC: small-duct (better prognosis) vs classic (large-duct) disease. Cholangiocarcinoma classified anatomically as intrahepatic, perihilar, and distal; gallbladder cancer staged as local vs advanced (ch.357 p.2731-2737; ch.355 p.2711; ch.87 p.667-670).
references: Harrison 22e ch.355 p.2710-2712 (PBC/PSC, Chronic Hepatitis & Cirrhosis)
Harrison 22e ch.87 p.667-670 (Cholangiocarcinoma and Gallbladder Cancer)
management: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy is the definitive treatment for symptomatic gallstone disease and its complications
Expectant management without surgery for asymptomatic gallstones, since most remain silent and prophylactic cholecystectomy is not warranted
ERCP with endoscopic sphincterotomy to clear common bile duct stones
Intravenous antibiotics and biliary decompression for acute cholangitis, with analgesia, fluids and supportive care for acute cholecystitis
Ursodeoxycholic acid or dietary and weight modification in selected patients unfit for surgery or to reduce bile lithogenicity
Cross-sectional imaging with MRCP or endoscopic ultrasound to define ductal stones before intervention
Referral to general or hepatobiliary surgery and gastroenterology as appropriate
